Mr. Mizanul Haque Chowdhury, with Mr. Hasan Rajib Prodhan, Advocates, ------ for petitioner.

parties:
M/S. Sonali Overseas
Vs.
The Commissioner of Customs and others
full_judgment:
7. During the course of argument we pointed out to Mr. Mizanul Haque Chowdhury that the impugned order is attracted by section 193 of the Customs Act i.e. the order is an appealable one and moreover it involves a disputed question of fact which could best be resolved in appeal by the parties before the appellate forum as provided by the Customs Act. On a query by us why the petitioner without resolving the dispute under section 193 of the Customs Act has moved this Court, the learned advocate could not say anything and he found it difficult to explain the situation. Then he made a submission that if we discharge the rule we should also give an observation to the effect that the petitioner may, if he so desires, file an appeal under section 193 of the Act before the appropriate appellate authority and in computing the limitation the period consumed before this court should be kept out of account. In support of his contention he relied on two unreported decisions of this court given in Writ Petition No. 3880 of 1998 and Writ petition No. 4312 of 2000. 

 9. In the other writ petition i.e. in Writ Petition No. 3880 of 1998 the petitioner moved the High Court Division under Article 102 (2) of the Constitution against an order passed by the Review Committee under section 193C of the Customs Act. But subsequently realized that the Writ Petition is not maintainable as an appeal lies against the Order of the Review Committee and as such filed an application for discharging the Rule for non-prosecution. At the time of hearing, the learned advocate further prayed that the time consumed in filing the Writ Petition may be excluded from the period of limitation as provided under section 196 of the Customs Act. The court in discharging the rule for non-prosecution observed. 

 "The period consumed before the High Court Division in moving this Writ Petition may be considered for exclusion in computing the period of limitation as provided under the Customs Act." 

 10. Now the pertinent question that falls for determination is as to whether this Court sitting in its writ jurisdiction can pass such an order. The admitted position is that the Customs Act is a special statute and the Limitation provided for by the Act is a special limitation and section 14 of the limitation Act which is a general law has no manner of application to the present case. Moreover, we have already found that the writ petition is incompetent and not maintainable for not availing of the alternative forum of appeal. If so, are we authorized by law to give any observation which will heavily weigh in the minds of the appellate authority. We are of the opinion that as soon as we find that the petition is incompetent and not maintainable the matter ends there and this court should follow the "hands off' doctrine and discharge the Rule and in such case there is no scope to give any observation to affect the statutory provision or merit of the case. If we give an observation the effect of which is to flout the provision of an Act, that would be an illegality by itself and we would be guilty of over stepping the authority vested in us by Article 102 of the Constitution. In the aforesaid two unreported decisions two different Division Benches of this Court in the course of dis charging the Rules observed that in computing the limitation the period spent before the High Court Division should be excluded. By their observations, in fact, the Court extended the period of limitation beyond the permissible limit allowed by the statute. With due respect we, therefore, find ourselves in difficulty to subscribe to those observations because in our opinion in giving those observations the Court has overlooked the provisions of section 193 of the Customs Act which is admittedly a special statue and a self contained one. Thus, the decisions appear to be in per currium i.e. in ignorance of law and as such not binding precedent. The decisions, therefore, have no binding force. In that view of the matter we refrain ourselves from giving any such direction to the Appellate Authority that in computing the period of limitation the time spent before this Court should be kept out of account, more so because that would override the statutory provision as contained in section 193 of the Customs Act and this Court sitting in its writ jurisdiction cannot arrogate to itself the power of the legislature and extend the period of limitation without any sanction of law. If such an observation is made it will not only lack the sanction of law but will greatly influence the minds of the Appellate Authority and consequently they will admit the appeal beyond time. The result would be disastrous. The Court is entrusted with the duty to dispense justice in accordance with law but it will be guilty of breaking the law. If the provisions of law is indiscriminately flouted by this Court that would lead to judicial anarchy and sow the seeds of confusion amongst the litigant public. The admitted position is that section 14 of the Limitation Act is not applicable in the instant case. Therefore, suffice it to say that he who chooses the sword must perish with the sword. Thus, we decline to make any such observation against the provision of law.
